title: Silas and the House
premise: Lior Ravensworth, a nonbinary hospice nurse in the dying village of Hollowmere, has always heard the dying count backwards—and always told himself it was coincidence. When the church bell that was melted down in 1911 begins to ring at dusk, Lior discovers the house he inherited from a grandmother he never met sits at the center of a covenant: the villagers traded one soul per generation for the bell's protection, and the last resident must sign the papers before the bell finishes singing its final verse. As Lior falls in love with the village archivist, Wren, and uncovers that his own name is already written in the covenant ledger, he must choose between duty to the dead who raised the house and the living self he is still becoming. In the end, Lior sings the last verse alone—not as a victim, but as a new author of the song—rewriting the covenant so the house keeps no one, and the bell finally falls silent.
about_author: Ada Sandoval is a former hospice volunteer from the Pacific Northwest who writes horror about the tenderness required at the edges of life. Her work has appeared in small-press anthologies, and Silas and the House is her first novel.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. During a night shift, Lior's patient counts backwards from one hundred and stops at zero exactly as she dies, whispering a word Lior refuses to write down. The emotional beat: quiet dread masked as professional calm, establishing Lior's habit of explaining away the inexplicable.

chapters.title: A Letter in Green Ink
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. A solicitor's letter announces Lior has inherited Ravensworth House from a grandmother no one ever mentioned. Lior burns the letter, then retrieves it from the ash. The beat: denial curdling into a pull he can't name.

chapters.title: Hollowmere at Dusk
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, arriving by bus. The village is picturesque but wrong—every clock stopped at 7:14, every garden grown to the same height. The beat: the uncanny welcome of a place that has been waiting.

chapters.title: The House That Breathes
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The house exhales when he unlocks it; dust falls upward. He finds a ledger on the hall table, open to a page with his name already inked. The beat: the first moment staying invisible stops being an option.

chapters.title: Wren of the Archive
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The village archivist catalogues the melted bell's fragments and notices a new entry appearing in the parish register overnight. Wren's curiosity is professional; her unease is not. The beat: the second witness arrives.

chapters.title: The Bell That Wasn't There
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. At 7:14 the church bell rings—though the tower is empty, the bell having been melted in 1911. Villagers don't look up. The beat: horror in the ordinary, the village's practiced deafness.

chapters.title: Explanations, Five Years of Them
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, flashback-tinged. Lior reviews his history of rationalizations for the backwards counting, and admits this house doesn't fit any of them. The beat: the collapse of a survival strategy.

chapters.title: The Ledger's Grammar
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren examines the ledger's script and finds the handwriting changes every few decades—each generation's hand, each generation's victim. The beat: scholarly dread, the shape of the covenant emerging.

chapters.title: Tea with Mrs. Aldous
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The oldest villager serves Lior tea and warns him, kindly, never to hum the bell's tune. She hums two bars before she can stop herself, and her nose begins to bleed. The beat: warmth laced with warning.

chapters.title: The Song's First Verse
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior dreams the bell's song and wakes with the first verse memorized, though he's never heard it awake. The house's walls are damp with condensation, as if sweating. The beat: the infection of the song.

chapters.title: What the Dying Know
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior returns briefly to the hospice; a dying man grabs his wrist and counts backwards, ending at the number seven—Lior's house number. The beat: the past and present covenant converging on him.

chapters.title: Wren's Question
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren confronts Lior at the churchyard: 'Do you know why you were sent for?' Their first real conversation becomes an argument becomes something warmer. The beat: connection sparking inside shared fear.

chapters.title: 1911, the Melting
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, archival documents and a found diary interleaved. The bell was melted to fund the war effort, but the diary reveals the villagers melted it to break the covenant—and failed, because the song lived on in the metal's memory. The beat: history as horror.

chapters.title: Silas
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior finds a child's room in the house, untouched for a century, with SILAS carved into the doorframe. The ledger's oldest entry is a boy of nine. The beat: grief for a stranger who feels like family.

chapters.title: The Papers
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The solicitor arrives with inheritance papers that are also covenant papers; the final page requires a signature in blood-warm ink. Lior signs the property transfer only, and the ink refuses to dry on the second page. The beat: the trap half-sprung.

chapters.title: Verse Two
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior catches himself humming verse two while making tea and stops mid-note; the house groans like a held breath released. Every mirror in the hall has fogged. The beat: the enemy is inside his own throat.

chapters.title: Wren's Ledger of Small Doubts
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren maps every covenant victim against village births and finds each was a child who didn't belong—an outsider, a foundling, someone the village never quite claimed. Like Lior. The beat: the pattern, and the tenderness of being seen.

chapters.title: The Harvest Supper
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The village holds a supper in Lior's honor; every dish is his favorite, though he told no one. Under the table, an old woman holds his hand and mouths: run. The beat: love and menace served on the same plate.

chapters.title: The House Remembers My Grandmother
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. In the attic Lior finds his grandmother's journals: she fled the house pregnant, spent her life hiding Lior's line from the ledger, and died counting backwards. The beat: inherited love as inherited debt.

chapters.title: Wren Breaks the Archive's Rule
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren removes the covenant's original parchment from the archive—forbidden—and copies it by hand through the night. The bell rings at 7:14 and she does not flinch. The beat: courage as an act of love.

chapters.title: The Third Verse Is a Name
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The song now plays in Lior's waking hours; he transcribes it and realizes verse three is a list of names, and the newest line is his own, half-faded, waiting for the signature. The beat: identity as the battlefield.

chapters.title: Mrs. Aldous at Zero
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Mrs. Aldous dies counting backwards, and at zero she says Lior's name. At the funeral, the entire village sings the first two verses in unison. The beat: the community's complicity made visible and terrible.

chapters.title: What Lior Refuses to Be
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior confronts his reflection, which sings along. He speaks his own name aloud—his chosen name, the one the ledger doesn't know—and the reflection's mouth stops moving. The beat: identity as resistance; the theme of selfhood weaponized.

chapters.title: The Bell's Hollow
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren descends into the bell tower's sealed base and finds the bell's melted remains fused into the foundation stone, still faintly warm after a century. The beat: the horror's physical heart located.

chapters.title: A Night of Two Beds
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior and Wren, exhausted and terrified, spend the night at the house—talking, then sleeping in the same room, not touching, then touching. The bell rings all night and neither of them hums. The beat: love as an anchor against the song.

chapters.title: The Village's Bargain, Retold
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren presents her findings to the village council: the covenant protected them from a famine winter in 1912, and they have paid for their safety with one stranger per generation ever since. Some council members already know. The beat: the banality of complicity.

chapters.title: The Last Resident
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior learns the legal phrase 'last resident' means the covenant's final signer—and the solicitor confirms the papers must be signed before the bell completes its verse. The bell is on verse three of four. The beat: the clock made audible.

chapters.title: Silas's Verse
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. In the child's room, Lior finally reads Silas's carved messages in the doorframe: a boy's counting, backwards, from one hundred, ending in a plea. Lior counts up from zero aloud, and the room warms. The beat: answering a century-old cry.

chapters.title: Wren Is Offered a Choice
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The council offers Wren the solicitor's role—keeper of the ledger—if she lets Lior sign alone. She sees her own name on a future page. The beat: temptation structured as duty.

chapters.title: The House Turns
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The house begins rearranging itself: doors lead to the past, hallways to 1911. Lior walks through a corridor and hears Silas's actual voice, singing. The beat: space itself becomes the antagonist.

chapters.title: Verse Four Begins
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The bell starts the final verse. Lior's hands move on their own, signing motions in the air; the ink on the unsigned page begins to rise like a tide. The beat: the body betraying the will.

chapters.title: The Council's Confession
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren forces the council to hear the ledger read aloud, name after name, and several elders admit their grandparents chose the victims. Shame splits the village; some want to end it, some need it to continue. The beat: a community breaking along its oldest fault line.

chapters.title: The Grandmother's Last Page
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior finds the final journal page, torn out, hidden in the bell tower: his grandmother's plan—'the song can be rewritten by whoever sings it last, willingly, in their own name.' The beat: hope discovered in the enemy's throat.

chapters.title: What the House Wants
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The house manifests his grandmother, or something wearing her voice, begging him to sign and rest. Lior recognizes the mimicry by what it gets wrong: it uses his deadname. The beat: grief weaponized, and defeated by self-knowledge.

chapters.title: Wren Chooses
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren burns her offered appointment and stands with Lior before the council, declaring the ledger a crime, not a covenant. Half the village walks out with them. The beat: duty redefined as love.

Lior's POV. The final verse reaches its last line. The house seals its doors, the ink floods the signature page, and the whole village stands in the churchyard watching the tower. The beat: the trap fully sprung, one breath before the climax.

chapters.title: The Last Verse, Sung
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Instead of refusing to sing, Lior sings the last verse—alone, willingly, in his own chosen name, changing the final line from 'keep' to 'free.' The bell's sound fractures, the ledger's ink runs backward, and Silas's counting finally reaches one and stops. The beat: the climax—love against duty, won by authorship.

chapters.title: The Silence After
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The bell is silent. The house exhales one last time and goes still, ordinary, cold. The village must live with what it was; some cannot, and leave. The beat: aftermath, grief without horror.

chapters.title: The Papers, Unsigned
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior tears the covenant page from the papers and buries it beneath the foundation stone beside the bell's remains, with Silas's name spoken aloud and, at last, a blessing. The beat: burial as reclamation.

chapters.title: A New Verse
chapters.summary: Lior and Wren, alternating. Months later, Lior still nurses the dying, and sometimes they still count backwards—but now he counts up with them, holding their hands, and no one is ever taken. In the garden, the house's clocks all tick at their own speeds, and Lior lets them. The beat: resolution—inheritance transformed into chosen belonging.
